compare.intro: To tell this unit's points apart, first ask which way the thing or the favour goes: あげる goes out from me to someone else, くれる comes in to me or my family, and with もらう I am the subject and the giver takes に or から; the te-forms (てあげる, てくれる, てもらう) follow the same directions for favours; てほしい only says that you want someone to do something, it does not ask them; and to ask someone in front of you, use てくれませんか or てもらえませんか with friends and coworkers, and go up to てくださいませんか or ていただけませんか for a teacher, a customer or a stranger.

forms.tag: わたしがする · I do it for them
forms.ja: [私|わたし]は友だちの[写真|しゃしん]をとって{あげました}。
forms.en: I took a photo of my friend for her.

forms.tag: ほかの人がしてくれる · they do it for me
forms.ja: 友だちが[私|わたし]の[写真|しゃしん]をとって{くれました}。
forms.en: My friend took a photo of me for me.

forms.tag: わたしがうける · I get it done
forms.ja: [私|わたし]は友だちに[写真|しゃしん]をとって{もらいました}。
forms.en: I had my friend take a photo of me.

check.label: セーターをほめられて
check.q: A：すてきなセーターですね。B：ありがとう。^[姉|あね]が[私|わたし]に^[作|つく]って（　　）んです。
why: てあげる goes out from my side to someone else. Here the sweater comes to 私に, so it cannot be あげた.
With てもらう the person who gets the favour is the subject, and the giver takes に. Here 姉が is the giver and 私に the receiver, so it cannot be もらった.
My sister (姉が) did it, and it came to me (私に): 作ってくれたんです. "My sister made it for me."

drill.label: Choose the form
drill.q: じしょを^わすれたので^、^[私|わたし]は^[田中|たなか]さんに[貸|か]して（　　）。
why: くれる needs someone else as the giver. Here 私は is the subject, so the sentence cannot end in くれました.
あげました would mean I lent my dictionary to Tanaka. But I forgot mine, so I am the one who got it.
いただけませんか asks the person you are talking to. This sentence tells what happened, so it needs a past ending.
I forgot my dictionary, so I (私は) got Tanaka (田中さんに) to lend me one: [貸|か]してもらいました.

drill.label: Choose the form
drill.q: （^先生^に）すみません、この[漢字|かんじ]の読み[方|かた]を[教|おし]えて（　　）。
why: くれ is a rough order, used only with close friends or family. Saying it to a teacher is rude.
You ask your teacher to do something for you, so you use the very polite いただけませんか.
[教|おし]えてほしいですか asks if the teacher wants someone to teach them. It is not a request.
[教|おし]えてあげませんか suggests the teacher teach someone else. You want them to teach you.

drill.label: Choose the form
drill.q: かぜで^[声|こえ]が出ません^から、だれかに[電話|でんわ]に出て（　　）。
why: 出てあげたい would mean I want to answer the phone for someone. But I have no voice.
With くれる the giver takes が, not に (だれかが出てくれます). And the sentence is about what I want.
I have no voice, so I want someone else to answer the phone: だれかに出てほしいです.
出てみたい is wanting to try it yourself. I have no voice, so I cannot.

drill.label: Choose the form
drill.q: （クラスの友だちに）すみません、^[私|わたし]たちの^[写真|しゃしん]をとって（　　）。
why: A polite request to a classmate, for us (私たちの写真): とってもらえませんか.
とってあげませんか suggests the friend take a photo for someone else. The photo is of us, for us.
とってほしいですか asks if the friend wants someone to take a photo. It is not a request.
いただきませんか is not used to ask for a favour. The request form is いただけませんか, and it is too polite for a classmate anyway.

drill.label: Build the sentence
drill.hint: Which tile finishes 買って, the favour I got from my father? The te-form goes right before ほしいです.
drill.full: 父に買ってもらった[時計|とけい]を{[弟|おとうと]にも}見てほしいです。
drill.explain: 父に買ってもらった describes [時計|とけい]: the watch my father bought me. [時計|とけい]を goes with 見て, and [弟|おとうと]にも names who I want to look at it: "I want my brother to see the watch my father bought me, too."

drill.label: Build the sentence
drill.hint: 友だちが is the giver, so which tile comes after かいて? The te-form goes right before いただけませんか.
drill.full: すみません、友だちがかいてくれた{[地図|ちず]を}見ていただけませんか。
drill.explain: 友だちがかいてくれた describes [地図|ちず]: the map my friend drew for me. [地図|ちず]を goes with 見て, and 見ていただけませんか is the polite request to a stranger: "Excuse me, could you look at this map my friend drew for me?"

exam.label: Choose the form
exam.q: （店で）店の人「プレゼントですか。」　わたし「はい、父に　（　　）んです。」
exam.explain: I am buying a present to give to my father, so it goes out from me: 父に　あげるんです. 父に　もらう would mean I get it from my father, but I am the one buying it. くれる is for things that come to me, and its giver takes が, not に. 父に　くれて　ほしい does not work: くれる is for things given to me, and its giver takes が.

exam.label: Choose the form
exam.q: 日本は　とても　きれいな　国です。いつか　家族にも　日本に　来て　（　　）。
exam.explain: I want my family to come to Japan some day: 家族にも　来て　ほしいです. 来て　あげたい would mean I come for someone, but here it is my family who comes. もらいました is past, but いつか is about the future. いただけませんか asks the person in front of you, and this sentence is not a request.

exam.label: Build the sentence
exam.before: これは　旅行の　とき　友だちに
exam.after: 見せて　あげたいです。
exam.full: これは　旅行の　とき　友だちに　とって　もらった　{写真で}　母にも　見せて　あげたいです。
exam.explain: とって, もらった, 写真で, 母にも. 友だちに　とって　もらった describes 写真: a photo my friend took for me. 写真で ends the first part ("this is a photo …, and"), and 母にも goes with 見せて　あげたい: "This is a photo a friend took for me on my trip, and I want to show it to my mother too."

scene.ja: ギフトショップのラッピングカウンター
scene.en: The wrapping counter at a gift shop
scene.intro: You are buying presents, and the wrapping counter has signs about wrapping and paying. Tap each word on them.

words.gloss: not free, there is a charge

check.label: How the exam asks it
check.q: 買った　_品物_は　べつべつに　つつんで　ください。
check.explain: 品物, goods, is read しなもの: both kanji take their Japanese reading here. 品 is ひん in some other words, and 物 is ぶつ in 動物, but ひんもの, しなぶつ and ひんぶつ are not words.

skill.ask: How much will the wrapping cost?
skill.passage:
ギフトショップ　さくら　ラッピングの　ごあんない
・きれいな　紙で　つつみます　……　百円
・リボンを　つけます　……　五十円
・はこに　入れます　……　二百円
・メッセージカード　……　無料
＊三千円以上　買った　方は、紙と　リボンが　無料に　なります。
＊^べつべつに　つつむ　ときは、一つずつ　料金が　かかります^。
＊ラッピングは　一かいの　カウンターで　どうぞ。
skill.strategy: Find the lines for what the customer wants, then read the notes with ＊: they change the price.

item.q: リンさんは　この　店で　千円の　ハンカチを　二まい　買いました。友だち　二人に　あげるので、べつべつに　紙で　つつんで、リボンも　つけて　ほしいです。ラッピングの　料金は　ぜんぶで　いくらですか。
item.explain: Paper is 百円 and a ribbon 五十円, and the note says each one wrapped separately is charged: (百円＋五十円)×2＝三百円.
why: Wrapping is free only after buying 三千円 or more. Lin bought two 千円 handkerchiefs, 二千円 in all.
百五十円 is paper and ribbon for one present. Lin wants two wrapped separately.
二百円 is paper for two presents, but Lin wants a ribbon on each too.
